title: Undecidability appears in almost any area of mathematics beyond easy questions

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Undecidability appears in almost any area of mathematics beyond easy questions

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Undecidability and unprovability will begin to occur in practically any area of mathematics almost as soon as one goes beyond questions that are always easy to answer, as a consequence of the Principle of Computational Equivalence.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: And indeed from the Principle of Computational Equivalence I strongly believe that in general undecidability and unprovability will start to occur in practically any area of mathematics almost as soon as one goes beyond the level of questions that are always easy to answer.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “Implications for Mathematics and Its Foundations” (from p. 772), p. 791. Scope: all areas of mathematics

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-37: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.35

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Published reductions resolve occurrence in many specific areas, so the claim has a testable core. Its near-universal and immediate-onset language has no fixed population or threshold and cannot be resolved by existing literature counts.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Select formal theories representing predefined mathematical areas and establish the complexity or undecidability boundary for decision problems within each. Decidable rich areas or delayed thresholds would refute restricted versions, while reductions establish occurrence in sampled areas.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Areas and the point beyond easy questions are undefined.

Literature coverage is not a representative sample of all mathematics.

Known decidable fragments complicate a universal threshold.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Surveys and problem libraries document undecidability in group theory, tilings, Diophantine equations, topology, and other fields, and they also document large decidable theories. That literature can test the pattern inside studied areas. It does not measure almost as soon as questions stop being easy across practically any area, because both the threshold and the inventory of areas are unspecified.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Assemble a list of mathematical areas and, in each, separate questions with decision procedures from questions reduced to the halting problem. The pattern supports the claim where undecidability begins immediately past the decidable fragment, and challenges it where a large intermediate band stays decidable.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A decidable theory with difficult questions counts as a counterexample only after easy is defined.

Always easy and practically any area are not formal thresholds.

Known undecidability results concentrate in fields logicians chose to encode computation into.
